title: Well and Room
premise: Folklorist Marguerite Galloway returns to the village of Hollowmere to record its songs, only to find the villagers refuse to sing any of them twice—and the imaginary friend from their childhood, a figure called the Tallyman, waiting on the porch exactly as they left him. The Galloway family's fortune was built on a bargain sealed at the old well: one member of each generation is 'counted' and taken, and the family survives by never being noticed. But Marguerite's three years of rationalizing the noises have made them visible, and the well, drained dry by their great-grandfather's cheating of the count, is refilling. To save their scattered family, Marguerite must gather every relative back to Hollowmere before the water rises, learn the true song the village has been refusing to finish, and pay—or outwit—a debt that has compounded for four generations. In the end, Marguerite sings the song twice themselves, offering their own name to the count, and the well takes not a life but the inheritance itself: the house crumbles into the rising water, leaving the family poor, alive, and finally free.
about_author: Emrys Ravensworth is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing oral histories in remote coastal villages before turning to fiction. They write horror about debts—financial, familial, and otherwise—that compound quietly until they come due.

chapters.title: The Song You Don't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Marguerite arrives in Hollowmere with recording equipment and academic detachment, interviewing elderly singers who cut off mid-verse whenever she raises her microphone. Her aunt Edith warns her off the well road. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: unease dressed up as professional curiosity.

chapters.title: What Waited on the Porch
chapters.summary: At the decaying Galloway house, Marguerite finds the Tallyman—a tall, patient figure from their childhood imaginings—sitting on the porch steps, unchanged after twenty years. He greets them by name and says, 'You're on the list now.' POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: the collapse of rational explanation.

chapters.title: Ledger of Small Noises
chapters.summary: Marguerite rereads three years of journal entries documenting knocks, dripping, and counting sounds, horrified to see the pattern they explained away: the noises were always counting down. A letter from their late mother surfaces, unfinished, beginning 'If you can hear him—'. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: dread of complicity.

chapters.title: Edith Remembers the Water Level
chapters.summary: Aunt Edith reveals the family secret obliquely: the well 'went dry' the year Marguerite's great-grandfather Aldous refused to give up his brother, and the family has been 'living quiet' ever since. She refuses to say what living quiet cost. POV: alternating Marguerite/Edith. Emotional beat: grief under deflection.

chapters.title: The Village That Won't Finish
chapters.summary: Marguerite records fragments of the Hollowmere song from six different singers; assembled, the verses describe a well that drinks names. When she plays the assembled version aloud in the pub, every villager leaves at once. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: isolation sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Brother, Absent
chapters.summary: Marguerite calls their estranged brother Caspian, a gambler in debt, who laughs off the warning until Marguerite mentions the Tallyman—and hears Caspian go silent, because he's seen him too, in mirrors. POV: Caspian. Emotional beat: fear cracking cynicism.

chapters.title: Aldous's Cheating Hand
chapters.summary: In the parish archive, Marguerite finds Aldous Galloway's 1911 diary: the well demanded a Galloway name each generation, and Aldous substituted a hired man's, buying the family forty years of stolen time. The diary's last page is wet. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: inherited guilt made concrete.

chapters.title: Counting in the Walls
chapters.summary: Back at the house, the Tallyman sits inside now, politely tallying aloud—names of every Galloway, living and dead. He reaches Marguerite's name and pauses, waiting for them to confirm it. Marguerite refuses, and every clock in the house stops. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: terror of acknowledgment.

chapters.title: Cousins in the Wind
chapters.summary: Marguerite begins calling the scattered family: cousin Wren in Glasgow, uncles in Canada, a niece nobody knew existed. Some hang up; some already hear counting. Wren agrees to come, bringing her daughter—the youngest Galloway. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: reluctant solidarity forming.

chapters.title: The Hired Man's Descendants
chapters.summary: Marguerite tracks down the family of Thomas Reeve, the man Aldous sacrificed. His great-granddaughter, a hard-faced woman named Ivy, has kept her own records—and her own visits from a different, hungrier figure. She wants in on whatever fix Marguerite plans. POV: Ivy. Emotional beat: righteous anger as an ally.

chapters.title: Water Where Water Wasn't
chapters.summary: The dry well behind the house is found brimming, black and still, though the water table hasn't shifted in decades. Fish float dead on its surface, arranged in rows. Edith sees it and finally tells everything: the count isn't cruelty, it's containment. POV: Edith. Emotional beat: the protective lie collapsing.

chapters.title: Living Quiet, Dying Loud
chapters.summary: Edith recounts how Marguerite's mother tried to end the bargain by moving away, and how the family's luck curdled wherever they settled until she came back and paid 'a partial amount.' Marguerite realizes their three years away are why the Tallyman found them. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: mourning reframed as consequence.

chapters.title: Assembly of the Named
chapters.summary: Nine Galloways arrive at Hollowmere for a reunion no one will admit is a summons. Old grievances flare—money, blame, the mother's death—but when the well audibly gulps at dusk, argument dies into common purpose. POV: ensemble, anchored on Caspian. Emotional beat: fractured family forced into a circle.

chapters.title: The Verse Nobody Wrote Down
chapters.summary: Ivy produces the missing final verse, preserved in the Reeve family as a curse: the song, sung complete and twice, doesn't summon the well—it settles accounts, naming a payer. The catch: whoever sings it offers their name first. POV: Ivy. Emotional beat: hope arriving with a price tag.

chapters.title: Rehearsal at Midnight
chapters.summary: The family attempts the full song together in the kitchen; voices fail at the last verse except Marguerite's, which carries alone and draws every light in the house toward the well. The Tallyman applauds softly from the doorway. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: terrible discovery of aptitude.

chapters.title: What Caspian Tried to Do
chapters.summary: Caspian, convinced he's the most expendable, goes to the well alone at 3 a.m. to sing the verse himself and settle the debt cheaply. The well rejects him—his name was already spent, gambled away in a dream he barely remembers. Marguerite drags him back half-drowned in nothing. POV: Caspian. Emotional beat: self-sacrifice meeting cosmic bureaucracy.

chapters.title: The Refill
chapters.summary: The well begins rising visibly, flooding the cellar, the ground floor, climbing the stairs like a tide with intent. The village below starts evacuating as Hollowmere's springs run backward. The Tallyman tells Marguerite the deadline plainly: all names gathered, or all names taken. POV: ensemble. Emotional beat: siege mentality.

chapters.title: Negotiation with a Hole
chapters.summary: Marguerite descends to the waterline and bargains—not to cancel the debt but to change its currency: not lives, but the inheritance itself, the house, the land, the name's claim on Hollowmere. The well considers. The Tallyman, for the first time, looks uncertain. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: defiance discovering leverage.

chapters.title: Sung Twice
chapters.summary: On the flooded threshold, Marguerite sings the complete song twice, alone, voice steady, offering the Galloway inheritance in place of a Galloway life. The family joins on the second pass—not to offer themselves but to witness. The well accepts, and begins to drink the house instead. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: climax—terror transmuted into ceremony.

chapters.title: The Taking of Galloway House
chapters.summary: The house folds into the well over a single night, stone drinking downward without splash or sound, while the family watches from the road. The Tallyman, his ledger balanced, tips his hat to Marguerite and becomes simply a shadow, then less. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: awe and bereavement entwined.

chapters.title: Poor and Unlisted
chapters.summary: Weeks later, the surviving Galloways—alive, landless, sharing a rented cottage—find that silence follows them nowhere anymore. No counting, no figures on porches. Ivy and the Reeves receive a formal apology written in Aldous's hand, delivered impossibly. POV: ensemble. Emotional beat: the strange lightness of having nothing left to lose.

chapters.title: The Song Sung Twice, Freely
chapters.summary: In Hollowmere's pub, Marguerite teaches the full song to the village, and this time the singers finish it, and sing it again, laughing. Marguerite records it, then deletes the recording—it belongs sung, not stored. On the walk home past the filled-in well, they hum, and nothing answers, and that is the whole miracle. POV: Marguerite. Emotional beat: resolution—survival redefined as freedom from the ledger.
